explanation: Other big cats sheathe their claws to keep them sharp. The cheetah's blunt, ever-ready claws grip like spikes, while a sharp dewclaw higher on each front leg hooks fleeing prey.

claims.text: A cheetah's claws are semi-retractable and stay partly exposed.
Leopards, lions and jaguars can fully retract their claws.
Big cats other than the cheetah retract their claws into protective sheaths, which keeps them sharp.
The cheetah's partly exposed claws are blunter than those of other big cats and give it grip when it runs.
Cheetahs use the sharp dewclaw on each front leg to hook or trip prey.

evidence.restatement: Cheetah claws retract only partly and have no protective sheath, so their tips always show.
Leopards, lions and jaguars, like other Panthera cats, have fully retractile claws.
In the other big cats the claws pull back into skin sheaths at rest, which protects their points from wear.
Because they always touch the ground, cheetah claws wear blunt and work like running spikes for traction in a sprint.
The cheetah's dewclaw, set higher on the inside of each foreleg, stays sharp and is used to hook or trip prey during a chase.
Cheetah claws can only be partly drawn back and are never fully sheathed, so they stay partly exposed.

claimResults.note: Semi-retractable is the standard description. 'Big cat' is an informal grouping that conventionally includes the cheetah.

evidence.restatement: Lions, leopards and jaguars can pull their claws fully back into skin sheaths.
Cats other than the cheetah draw the claws into sheaths, which protects the tips from wear.
Cheetah claws are straighter and blunter than a lion's or leopard's and act like running spikes for grip.
The cheetah's sharp dewclaw on each front leg is used to hook or trip fleeing prey.

stem: Which big cat's claws stay partly out at all times, gripping the ground like a sprinter's spikes?
